flawed_step: The claim assumes that a tree's degree sequence fixes the tree up to isomorphism. It does not: it leaves open which degrees sit next to each other.
counterexample:
Tree A has vertices c, a1, a2, b1, b2 and d, with edges c-a1, a1-a2, c-b1, b1-b2 and c-d. It has 6 vertices, 5 edges and is connected, so it is a tree. Its degrees are c=3, a1=2, b1=2, a2=1, b2=1 and d=1, giving the sequence (3,2,2,1,1,1).

Tree B has vertices c, a1, a2, a3, b and d, with edges c-a1, a1-a2, a2-a3, c-b and c-d. It also has 6 vertices, 5 edges and is connected, so it is a tree. Its degrees are c=3, a1=2, a2=2, a3=1, b=1 and d=1, giving the same sequence (3,2,2,1,1,1).

An isomorphism keeps each vertex's degree and keeps adjacency. So it would have to send the only degree-3 vertex of A to the only degree-3 vertex of B, and the number of degree-2 neighbours of that vertex could not change. In A, c has two degree-2 neighbours (a1 and b1). In B, c has one (a1). So A and B are not isomorphic.
assessment_summary: These two six-vertex trees disprove the claim. A is a degree-3 vertex with branches of lengths 2, 2 and 1. B is a degree-3 vertex with branches of lengths 3, 1 and 1. Both have degree sequence (3,2,2,1,1,1). In A the degree-3 vertex has two degree-2 neighbours, but in B it has only one, and an isomorphism cannot change that. So the trees are not isomorphic.
